newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana drivers get license to shoot carjackers.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana drivers get license to shoot carjackers.

text.p: Would-be carjackers may face a serious threat in Louisiana starting on Friday when a new law takes effect allowing intended victims to shoot to kill.

The "shoot-the-carjacker" law, approved by the state legislature earlier this summer, is a companion to the 1993 "shoot the burglar" law that allowed residents to open fire when they believe themselves to be in danger from an intruder.
"I think it will serve as a deterrent -- it's a strong message -- to people out there when they know their victims can justifiably defend themselves," State Police Lt. Mike Edmondson said.

"With more people aware of this law, it may save some lives," he said, but only if the letter of the law is followed. "This applies only to someone inside a vehicle who believes he or she is imminent danger."
John Vern of Lake Charles, La., a spokesman for the Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, said on Wednesday that his group opposed the politically popular law.

"We felt this was pretty dangerous in that it gives the public a perception that they should run out and get guns and carry them in their cars to defend themselves, when in fact, there are not a great many cases like this at all," Vern said.
"The law," he said, "does not necessarily provide the right to shoot and kill anyone who tries to take your car. It does not apply if you see someone stealing your car from your garage."

Although no statistics appear to have been kept on the number of shootings of intruders since the 1993 burglar bill passed, one case garnered worldwide attention when a Japanese exchange student was shot to death by a homeowner after the youth knocked on the wrong door looking for a party.
Although the homeowner was acquitted of criminal charges, the teenager's parents won a civil suit against him.
